claim: Most GWAS hits are located in cis-regulatory regions.
source: Most GWAS hits are located in cis-regulatory regions, but the underlying causal variants and their molecular mechanisms remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about GWAS hits.

claim: The underlying causal variants and their molecular mechanisms for most GWAS hits remain unknown.
source: Most GWAS hits are located in cis-regulatory regions, but the underlying causal variants and their molecular mechanisms remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a current limitation in the field.

claim: The study mapped quantitative trait loci for chromatin accessibility (caQTLs) in 1000 individuals from 10 diverse populations.
source: To better understand human cis-regulatory variation, we mapped quantitative trait loci for chromatin accessibility (caQTLs)—a key step in cis-regulation—in 1000 individuals from 10 diverse populations.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study design and sample size in the abstract.

claim: Most caQTLs were shared across populations.
source: Most caQTLs were shared across populations, allowing us to leverage the genetic diversity to fine-map candidate causal regulatory variants, several thousand of which have been previously implicated in GWAS.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Several thousand fine-mapped candidate causal regulatory variants have been previously implicated in GWAS.
source: Most caQTLs were shared across populations, allowing us to leverage the genetic diversity to fine-map candidate causal regulatory variants, several thousand of which have been previously implicated in GWAS.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a result of the fine-mapping analysis.

claim: Many caQTLs that affect the expression of distal genes also alter the landscape of long-range chromosomal interactions.
source: In addition, many caQTLs that affect the expression of distal genes also alter the landscape of long-range chromosomal interactions, suggesting a mechanism for long-range expression QTLs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Alterations in long-range chromosomal interactions suggest a mechanism for long-range expression QTLs.
source: In addition, many caQTLs that affect the expression of distal genes also alter the landscape of long-range chromosomal interactions, suggesting a mechanism for long-range expression QTLs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: GWAS have successfully mapped thousands of loci associated with hundreds of human diseases and other traits.
source: Indeed, these studies have successfully mapped thousands of loci associated with hundreds of human diseases and other traits (Eicher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The vast majority of causal variants that drive GWAS associations remain unknown.
source: However, the vast majority of causal variants that drive the associations remain unknown, since GWAS resolution is limited by the correlations between nearby variants known as linkage disequilibrium (LD).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of GWAS.

claim: GWAS resolution is limited by linkage disequilibrium (LD).
source: However, the vast majority of causal variants that drive the associations remain unknown, since GWAS resolution is limited by the correlations between nearby variants known as linkage disequilibrium (LD).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an explanation for why causal variants remain unknown.

claim: Pinpointing causal variants is essential for accurately predicting disease risk.
source: Pinpointing causal variants is essential not only for accurately predicting disease risk, but also for understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie complex trait variation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for the study.

claim: Pinpointing causal variants is essential for understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie complex trait variation.
source: Pinpointing causal variants is essential not only for accurately predicting disease risk, but also for understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie complex trait variation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for the study.

claim: Even the largest GWAS studies have yielded only a few dozen causal variants.
source: Increasing GWAS sample size or genotyping density can improve resolution, but even the largest studies have yielded only a few dozen causal variants (Farh et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Trans-ethnic fine-mapping is an alternative to increasing sample size within a single population for achieving high mapping resolution.
source: To achieve high mapping resolution, an alternative to increasing sample size within a single population is trans-ethnic fine-mapping, in which a GWAS is performed across multiple populations (van de Bunt et al., 2015; Asimit et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the approach.

claim: Shared causal variants should be consistently associated with a trait across populations.
source: Shared causal variants should be consistently associated with a trait across populations, while tag SNPs—those associated only because of their LD with a causal variant—may only be associated in a subset of populations, due to differing LD structures.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the principle behind trans-ethnic fine-mapping.

claim: Tag SNPs may only be associated in a subset of populations due to differing LD structures.
source: Shared causal variants should be consistently associated with a trait across populations, while tag SNPs—those associated only because of their LD with a causal variant—may only be associated in a subset of populations, due to differing LD structures.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the principle behind trans-ethnic fine-mapping.

claim: Trans-ethnic fine-mapping is especially effective when combining populations with disparate LD patterns, such as Europeans and Africans.
source: This approach is especially effective when combining populations with disparate LD patterns, such as Europeans and Africans (Asimit et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Most GWAS have been restricted to European cohorts.
source: However, most GWAS have been restricted to European cohorts, limiting not only their mapping resolution, but also their ability to predict disease risk in non-European individuals (Hindorff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The restriction of most GWAS to European cohorts limits their mapping resolution.
source: However, most GWAS have been restricted to European cohorts, limiting not only their mapping resolution, but also their ability to predict disease risk in non-European individuals (Hindorff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The restriction of most GWAS to European cohorts limits their ability to predict disease risk in non-European individuals.
source: However, most GWAS have been restricted to European cohorts, limiting not only their mapping resolution, but also their ability to predict disease risk in non-European individuals (Hindorff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: QTLs involved in cis-regulation are especially informative because the vast majority of GWAS hits are in noncoding regions.
source: QTLs involved in cis-regulation are especially informative, since the vast majority of GWAS hits are in noncoding regions (Hindorff et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: eQTLs are enriched for SNPs implicated by GWAS in a wide range of diseases.
source: For example, QTLs for mRNA levels (eQTLs) are enriched for SNPs implicated by GWAS in a wide range of diseases, suggesting specific genes as likely mediators of the associations (Lappalainen et al., 2013; Battle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Similar enrichments have been reported for QTLs affecting mRNA splicing.
source: Similar enrichments have been reported for QTLs affecting mRNA splicing (Fraser and Xie, 2009; Li et al., 2016), transcription factor binding (Waszak et al., 2015; Tehranchi et al., 2016), and chromatin accessibility (Kumasaka et al., 2016; Gate et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Similar enrichments have been reported for QTLs affecting transcription factor binding.
source: Similar enrichments have been reported for QTLs affecting mRNA splicing (Fraser and Xie, 2009; Li et al., 2016), transcription factor binding (Waszak et al., 2015; Tehranchi et al., 2016), and chromatin accessibility (Kumasaka et al., 2016; Gate et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Similar enrichments have been reported for QTLs affecting chromatin accessibility.
source: Similar enrichments have been reported for QTLs affecting mRNA splicing (Fraser and Xie, 2009; Li et al., 2016), transcription factor binding (Waszak et al., 2015; Tehranchi et al., 2016), and chromatin accessibility (Kumasaka et al., 2016; Gate et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Nearly all molecular-level QTL studies have been limited to a single population.
source: However, nearly all of these molecular-level QTL studies have been limited to a single population (most often either Europeans or Yorubans), thus limiting their utility for understanding worldwide human diversity—similar to the bias of GWAS for Europeans.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of previous studies.

claim: Pooling samples prior to sequencing minimizes experimental variability between samples.
source: This pooling minimizes experimental variability between samples (both within and between experimental 'batches'), reducing the cost and effort of QTL mapping by over 25-fold compared to standard unpooled approaches (Tehranchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Pooling reduces the cost and effort of QTL mapping by over 25-fold compared to standard unpooled approaches.
source: This pooling minimizes experimental variability between samples (both within and between experimental 'batches'), reducing the cost and effort of QTL mapping by over 25-fold compared to standard unpooled approaches (Tehranchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The study selected a total of 1000 lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) with full genome sequences from 10 diverse populations.
source: We selected a total of 1000 lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) with full genome sequences (Auton et al., 2015) from 10 diverse populations: four European, four African, one African-American, and one Han Chinese (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the study design.

claim: The 10 diverse populations included four European, four African, one African-American, and one Han Chinese.
source: We selected a total of 1000 lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) with full genome sequences (Auton et al., 2015) from 10 diverse populations: four European, four African, one African-American, and one Han Chinese (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the study design.

claim: The study combined 66–112 unrelated individuals from each population into one pool per population.
source: We combined 66–112 unrelated individuals from each population into one pool per population, and performed ATAC-seq with two biological replicates per population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), resulting in a total of ~808 million informative autosomal reads from 20 pools.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the experimental design.

claim: The study performed ATAC-seq with two biological replicates per population.
source: We combined 66–112 unrelated individuals from each population into one pool per population, and performed ATAC-seq with two biological replicates per population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), resulting in a total of ~808 million informative autosomal reads from 20 pools.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the experimental design.

claim: The study resulted in a total of ~808 million informative autosomal reads from 20 pools.
source: We combined 66–112 unrelated individuals from each population into one pool per population, and performed ATAC-seq with two biological replicates per population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), resulting in a total of ~808 million informative autosomal reads from 20 pools.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the data generated.

claim: All populations showed a high correlation between pre-ATAC and post-ATAC allele frequencies (average Pearson r = 0.92).
source: All populations showed a high correlation between pre-ATAC and post-ATAC allele frequencies (average Pearson r = 0.92; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), as expected if most SNPs do not affect CA and thus have similar pre- and post-ATAC frequencies (Tehranchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: At a nominal p<5×10−4, the study mapped 13,657 to 26,182 independent caQTLs per population.
source: At a nominal p<5×10−4—corresponding to an irreproducible discovery rate (IDR, analogous to a false discovery rate; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) of ~1%—we mapped 13,657 to 26,182 independent caQTLs per population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the caQTL mapping results.

claim: A nominal p<5×10−4 corresponds to an irreproducible discovery rate (IDR) of ~1%.
source: At a nominal p<5×10−4—corresponding to an irreproducible discovery rate (IDR, analogous to a false discovery rate; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) of ~1%—we mapped 13,657 to 26,182 independent caQTLs per population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the IDR analysis.

claim: The caQTLs comprised 1.5–3.0% of all testable SNPs.
source: This comprised 1.5–3.0% of all testable SNPs, defined as those with >2% minor allele frequency (MAF) and covered by at least 20 reads (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: A total of 126,773 caQTLs were significant in at least one population.
source: A total of 126,773 caQTLs were significant in at least one population (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the total number of caQTLs identified.

claim: There is a 33- to 76-fold enrichment of dsQTLs among caQTLs, with highest enrichment in the five African/African-American populations.
source: We found a 33- to 76-fold enrichment of dsQTLs among caQTLs, with highest enrichment in the five African/African-American populations (Figure 1C; enrichments for other QTLs in Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures showing the enrichment analysis.

claim: The quantitative effect sizes of caQTLs and dsQTLs show excellent agreement (Pearson r = 0.85).
source: Second, we compared the quantitative effect sizes of caQTLs and dsQTLs, and found excellent agreement (Pearson r = 0.85; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the correlation.

claim: Directionality agreement between caQTLs and dsQTLs reached 96.7–98.1% at caQTL p<5×10−4.
source: Third, we tested how the directionality agreement (whether caQTLs and dsQTLs call the same allele as more accessible) changes with the caQTL p-value, and found that agreement increased with more stringent cutoffs, reaching 96.7–98.1% agreement at caQTL p<5×10−4 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the directionality agreement.

claim: Directionality agreement between caQTLs and bQTLs reached 97.3–98.9% at caQTL p<5×10−4.
source: Once again, we found that the agreement increases with more stringent p-value cutoffs, reaching 97.3–98.9% agreement at caQTL p<5×10−4 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the directionality agreement.

claim: The high level of agreement between caQTLs and bQTLs suggests a low rate of false positive caQTLs, consistent with the estimated 1% IDR.
source: This high level of agreement suggests a low rate of false positive caQTLs, consistent with our estimated 1% IDR.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the directionality agreement results.

claim: At a matched cutoff in the CEU population, the study mapped 2.8-fold more caQTLs with 15-fold fewer reads and 12-fold fewer ATAC-seq libraries compared to RASQUAL.
source: At a matched cutoff in our CEU population, we mapped 2.8-fold more caQTLs with 15-fold fewer reads and 12-fold fewer ATAC-seq libraries—a ~ 40 fold improvement in cost per caQTL (see Supplemental Note).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison with a previous study.

claim: The pooling approach resulted in a ~40 fold improvement in cost per caQTL compared to RASQUAL.
source: At a matched cutoff in our CEU population, we mapped 2.8-fold more caQTLs with 15-fold fewer reads and 12-fold fewer ATAC-seq libraries—a ~ 40 fold improvement in cost per caQTL (see Supplemental Note).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison with a previous study.

claim: The mean fraction of shared caQTLs was 59.9% within Africans.
source: Among these, we observed a clear trend for increased sharing within continents: the mean fraction of shared caQTLs was 59.9% within Africans and 59.8% within Europeans, compared to 48.4% between these two groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the sharing analysis.

claim: The mean fraction of shared caQTLs was 59.8% within Europeans.
source: Among these, we observed a clear trend for increased sharing within continents: the mean fraction of shared caQTLs was 59.9% within Africans and 59.8% within Europeans, compared to 48.4% between these two groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the sharing analysis.

claim: The mean fraction of shared caQTLs was 48.4% between Africans and Europeans.
source: Among these, we observed a clear trend for increased sharing within continents: the mean fraction of shared caQTLs was 59.9% within Africans and 59.8% within Europeans, compared to 48.4% between these two groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the sharing analysis.

claim: Han Chinese (CHB) caQTLs were shared moderately with Europeans (52.4%).
source: The Han Chinese (CHB) caQTLs were shared moderately with Europeans (52.4%) and less well with Africans (47.7%), reflecting their closer relatedness to Europeans.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the sharing patterns.

claim: Han Chinese (CHB) caQTLs were shared less well with Africans (47.7%).
source: The Han Chinese (CHB) caQTLs were shared moderately with Europeans (52.4%) and less well with Africans (47.7%), reflecting their closer relatedness to Europeans.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the sharing patterns.

claim: African-American (ASW) caQTLs showed greater sharing with all five European/Han populations than any of the four African populations did.
source: In addition, African-American (ASW) caQTLs showed greater sharing with all five European/Han populations than any of the four African populations did, consistent with their admixed ancestry.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the sharing patterns.

claim: The concordance between caQTL sharing and known phylogenetic relationships suggests that some caQTLs may have population-specific effects.
source: The concordance between caQTL sharing and known phylogenetic relationships suggests that some caQTLs may have population-specific effects, as has also been observed for other types of molecular QTLs (Stranger et al., 2012; Fraser et al., 2012), though the biological mechanisms underlying this divergence will require further study.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the interpretation.

claim: There is increasing enrichment for known causal variants with increasing number of significant caQTL populations.
source: We found increasing enrichment for known causal variants with increasing number of significant caQTL populations (Figure 2C), suggesting that combining the diverse LD patterns improved our mapping resolution substantially.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the enrichment analysis.

claim: Combining diverse LD patterns improved mapping resolution substantially.
source: We found increasing enrichment for known causal variants with increasing number of significant caQTL populations (Figure 2C), suggesting that combining the diverse LD patterns improved our mapping resolution substantially.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the enrichment analysis.

claim: At a combined p<5×10−6, the study identified 45,243 SNPs as shared caQTLs.
source: In order to account for both the number of significant populations as well as the caQTL strength within each population (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), we calculated Fisher's combined p-value for each caQTL across all ten populations; at a combined p<5×10−6, we identified 45,243 SNPs, which we refer to as 'shared caQTLs' (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the fine-mapping approach.

claim: Nearly all (99.8%) of the shared caQTLs were significant across multiple populations.
source: Nearly all (99.8%) of these were significant across multiple populations, and 98.6% showed concordance of the more accessible allele across populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the shared caQTLs.

claim: 98.6% of shared caQTLs showed concordance of the more accessible allele across populations.
source: Nearly all (99.8%) of these were significant across multiple populations, and 98.6% showed concordance of the more accessible allele across populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the shared caQTLs.

claim: Shared caQTLs were most highly enriched near active enhancers and transcription start sites (TSSs), accounting for 54% of shared caQTLs in just 3.1% of the genome.
source: We found that they were most highly enriched near active enhancers and transcription start sites (TSSs) (Ernst and Kellis, 2012), accounting for 54% of shared caQTLs in just 3.1% of the genome (Figure 3A, purple and dark green).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the genomic location analysis.

claim: After controlling for read density, the strongest enrichments were found in weak enhancers (2.3-fold) and quiescent regions (3.6-fold).
source: However, these enrichments were primarily driven by ATAC-seq read density, reflecting greater chromatin accessibility in these regions; after controlling for read density, we found the strongest enrichments in weak enhancers (2.3-fold) and quiescent regions (3.6-fold), and 8.7-fold depletion near TSSs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the genomic location analysis after controlling for read density.

claim: After controlling for read density, there was an 8.7-fold depletion of shared caQTLs near TSSs.
source: However, these enrichments were primarily driven by ATAC-seq read density, reflecting greater chromatin accessibility in these regions; after controlling for read density, we found the strongest enrichments in weak enhancers (2.3-fold) and quiescent regions (3.6-fold), and 8.7-fold depletion near TSSs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the genomic location analysis after controlling for read density.

claim: Mutations affecting accessibility near TSSs are more likely to be deleterious and thus selected against, resulting in the observed depletion.
source: We hypothesize that mutations affecting accessibility near TSSs are more likely to be deleterious, and thus selected against, resulting in the observed depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis to explain the depletion near TSSs.

claim: The 8.7-fold depletion near TSSs is greater than the analogous depletion of nonsynonymous changes in exons.
source: This 8.7-fold depletion near TSSs is greater than the analogous depletion of nonsynonymous changes in exons; in fact, we estimated that that these caQTLs are ~81% more likely to be deleterious, and removed by selection, than nonsynonymous mutations (see Supplemental Note).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison with nonsynonymous mutations.

claim: caQTLs near TSSs are ~81% more likely to be deleterious and removed by selection than nonsynonymous mutations.
source: This 8.7-fold depletion near TSSs is greater than the analogous depletion of nonsynonymous changes in exons; in fact, we estimated that that these caQTLs are ~81% more likely to be deleterious, and removed by selection, than nonsynonymous mutations (see Supplemental Note).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an estimate based on the comparison with nonsynonymous mutations.

claim: caQTLs near active TSSs have lower minor allele frequencies than elsewhere in the genome (median MAF = 0.17 for active TSS regions compared to 0.21 for caQTLs elsewhere).
source: Consistent with this, we also found that caQTLs near active TSSs have lower minor allele frequencies than elsewhere in the genome (median MAF = 0.17 for active TSS regions and 0.18 for flanking active TSS regions, compared to 0.21 for caQTLs elsewhere; Wilcoxon p=1.5×10−28 and 8 × 10−6 respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical tests to support the claim.

claim: The study found 80 known TF motifs enriched in the open allele sequences (FDR ≤ 0.1% for each).
source: We found 80 known TF motifs enriched in the open allele sequences (FDR ≤ 0.1% for each; Figure 3B), but none enriched in the closed alleles from the same caQTL loci.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the motif analysis.

claim: No TF motifs were enriched in the closed alleles from the same caQTL loci.
source: We found 80 known TF motifs enriched in the open allele sequences (FDR ≤ 0.1% for each; Figure 3B), but none enriched in the closed alleles from the same caQTL loci.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the motif analysis results.

claim: The striking asymmetry in motif enrichment supports the idea that a major mechanism leading to caQTLs is disruption of TF binding.
source: This striking asymmetry supports the idea that a major mechanism leading to caQTLs is disruption of TF binding, where caQTL variants matching the consensus motif—and thus promoting TF binding—result in more accessible chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the motif enrichment results.

claim: The caQTL density is strongly correlated with the information content of each CTCF motif position (Pearson r = 0.86).
source: Comparing shared caQTL density with the CTCF motif, we indeed found that the caQTL density is strongly correlated with the information content of each motif position (Pearson r = 0.86; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the correlation.

claim: Shared caQTLs cause small but significant differences in DNA shape compared to non-caQTL variants matched for ATAC-seq read depth.
source: We found small but significant differences in how caQTLs impact DNA shape (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) suggesting that DNA shape may contribute to variation in CA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the DNA shape analysis.

claim: DNA shape may contribute to variation in chromatin accessibility.
source: We found small but significant differences in how caQTLs impact DNA shape (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) suggesting that DNA shape may contribute to variation in CA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the DNA shape analysis.

claim: There is a 2.5-fold enrichment of the more accessible allele having more long-range interactions (>20 kb away).
source: To test if caQTLs also affect long-range interactions, we measured how often the more accessible allele had significantly more long-range interactions (with loci > 20 kb away) (Rao et al., 2014) than the less accessible allele, and vice versa; we found a 2.5-fold enrichment of the more accessible allele having more interactions (Figure 4A; binomial p<10−36), similar to the 2.2-fold bias of CTCF bQTLs (Tehranchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure and statistical test.

claim: The allelic ratio increased slightly to 2.7-fold when restricted to interactions > 100 kb apart.
source: The allelic ratio increased slightly (to 2.7-fold) when restricted to interactions > 100 kb apart.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the long-range interaction analysis.

claim: The enrichment for long-range interactions was not observed for inter-chromosomal interactions.
source: This enrichment was not observed for inter-chromosomal interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting it is unlikely to be due to a nonspecific bias in the Hi-C assay.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the control analysis.

claim: The results establish a role for chromatin accessibility in polymorphic long-range chromosomal interactions of a similar magnitude as CTCF.
source: These results establish a role for CA in polymorphic long-range chromosomal interactions of a similar magnitude as CTCF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the long-range interaction analysis.

claim: bQTLs that affect chromatin accessibility show a strong and consistent effect on long-range interactions (binomial p<0.008 for each TF).
source: We found a strong and consistent effect on long-range interactions for bQTLs that affect accessibility, in which the allele with increased TF binding is biased towards having more interactions (Figure 4B left; binomial p<0.008 for each).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: bQTLs that do not affect chromatin accessibility show no significant effect on long-range interactions (binomial p>0.08 for all six TFs).
source: In contrast, we found no significant effect for the bQTLs that do not affect accessibility, for all six TFs (Figure 4B right; binomial p>0.08 for each).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: TF binding alone has no detectable association with long-range interactions; even for CTCF, an effect on chromatin accessibility is also necessary.
source: This suggests that TF binding alone has no detectable association with long-range interactions; even for CTCF, an effect on CA is also necessary.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the bQTL analysis.

claim: Chromatin accessibility is a key intermediary between TF binding and chromosomal interactions.
source: Together with additional evidence (See Supplemental Note), we propose that CA is a key intermediary between TF binding and chromosomal interactions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a proposed model based on the analyses.

claim: caQTLs were strongly enriched for local eQTLs (TSS <10 kb from the caQTL) (Fisher's exact p<10−300).
source: As expected, we found that overall caQTLs were strongly enriched for local eQTLs (TSS <10 kb from the caQTL); restricting the analysis to caQTLs with no effect on interactions reduced the magnitude of this enrichment, but it was still highly significant in both cases (Figure 4C left; Fisher's exact p<10−300 for each enrichment), suggesting that changes in long-range interactions are not necessary for caQTLs to affect transcription of nearby genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: Changes in long-range interactions are not necessary for caQTLs to affect transcription of nearby genes.
source: As expected, we found that overall caQTLs were strongly enriched for local eQTLs (TSS <10 kb from the caQTL); restricting the analysis to caQTLs with no effect on interactions reduced the magnitude of this enrichment, but it was still highly significant in both cases (Figure 4C left; Fisher's exact p<10−300 for each enrichment), suggesting that changes in long-range interactions are not necessary for caQTLs to affect transcription of nearby genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the eQTL enrichment analysis.

claim: caQTLs were enriched for distal eQTLs (p<10−70), but this enrichment was entirely lost when restricting the analysis to caQTLs with no change in long-range interactions (p=0.20).
source: caQTLs were also enriched for distal eQTLs (p<10−70), but this enrichment was entirely lost when restricting the analysis to caQTLs with no change in long-range interactions (Figure 4C right; p=0.20).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: Alterations in the patterns of long-range chromosomal interactions are necessary for caQTLs to affect distal gene expression.
source: This suggests that alterations in the patterns of long-range chromosomal interactions are necessary for caQTLs to affect distal gene expression (Figure 4D), and therefore that these polymorphic interactions may be an important mechanism by which eQTLs can act over vast genomic distances.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the eQTL enrichment analysis.

claim: Polymorphic long-range chromosomal interactions may be an important mechanism by which eQTLs can act over vast genomic distances.
source: This suggests that alterations in the patterns of long-range chromosomal interactions are necessary for caQTLs to affect distal gene expression (Figure 4D), and therefore that these polymorphic interactions may be an important mechanism by which eQTLs can act over vast genomic distances.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the eQTL enrichment analysis.

claim: For several autoimmune diseases, shared caQTLs were highly enriched for likely causal variants.
source: We found that for several autoimmune diseases—the class of disease most directly relevant to LCLs—shared caQTLs were highly enriched for likely causal variants (e.g. for Crohn's disease, mean causal probability for shared caQTLs was 2.4-fold higher than for non-caQTLs, p=0.002; for ankylosing spondylitis, mean causal probability for shared caQTLs was 2.6-fold higher, p=0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical tests to support the claim.

claim: rs4409785 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, and vitiligo.
source: In rare cases, a lack of LD allows GWAS to implicate a single likely causal variant; this is the case for rs4409785, which is associated with rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, and vitiligo (Sawcer et al., 2011; Jin et al., 2012, Okada et al., 2014), and was predicted to be the causal variant for vitiligo with 85% probability (Farh et al., 2015) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: rs4409785 is bound by CTCF in LCLs and disrupts a CTCF motif.
source: The SNP is bound by CTCF in LCLs (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) and disrupts a CTCF motif; we found that it is a caQTL in two European populations (FIN and TSI, p<3×10−6 in each; not tested in African or ASW populations due to its low MAF), thus providing evidence of an effect on accessibility that is likely mediated by CTCF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The study found 5598 caQTLs that were also associated with disease risk or other complex traits (GWAS p<5×10−8).
source: More broadly, we found 5598 caQTLs that were also associated with disease risk or other complex traits (GWAS p<5×10−8; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the GWAS overlaps.

claim: There are only ~2.2 caQTLs per GWAS locus, providing a far smaller credible set for targeted follow-up studies.
source: Although most GWAS loci include dozens of potential causal variants in LD, there are only ~2.2 caQTLs per GWAS locus, providing a far smaller credible set for targeted follow-up studies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the fine-mapping resolution.

claim: Among the caQTLs associated with GWAS traits, 115 caQTLs were shared across all ten populations.
source: Among these, 115 caQTLs were shared across all ten populations, suggesting that many of these are likely to be causal for disease risk; we highlight ten examples in Table 1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the most highly shared caQTLs.

claim: The regulatory effects of caQTLs are typically shared across most tissues.
source: Consistent with this, we found that the regulatory effects of caQTLs are typically shared across most tissues, suggesting that their effects on CA are broadly shared as well (Supplemental Note, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a supplemental note and figure.

claim: caQTLs measured in LCLs can contribute to risk for diseases that have no clear connection to LCLs.
source: Therefore, it should not be surprising that these caQTLs can contribute to risk for diseases that have no clear connection to LCLs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the tissue-sharing analysis.

claim: Molecular QTL mapping provides information about molecular mechanisms and allelic effect direction.
source: More generally, our results show that molecular QTL mapping and trans-ethnic fine-mapping are complementary in several respects. Molecular QTL mapping provides information about molecular mechanisms and allelic effect direction, while including multiple populations allows for fine-mapping of causal variants; combined, these can provide unprecedented insights into the genetic basis of human variation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the complementary approaches.

claim: Including multiple populations allows for fine-mapping of causal variants.
source: More generally, our results show that molecular QTL mapping and trans-ethnic fine-mapping are complementary in several respects. Molecular QTL mapping provides information about molecular mechanisms and allelic effect direction, while including multiple populations allows for fine-mapping of causal variants; combined, these can provide unprecedented insights into the genetic basis of human variation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the complementary approaches.

claim: Variation in molecular-level traits such as chromatin accessibility can be mapped to over 10^5 QTLs.
source: Moreover, since variation in molecular-level traits such as CA can be mapped to over 105 QTLs, they provide tremendous opportunities for fine-mapping regulatory variants throughout the genome, which can then inform follow-up studies for diseases or other traits where trans-ethnic fine-mapping may not be feasible (e.g. Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the opportunities provided by molecular QTL mapping.

claim: The study's results suggest that TF binding affects long-range chromosomal interactions via its effect on chromatin accessibility.
source: Our results suggest that TF binding affects long-range chromosomal interactions via its effect on CA, and that CA affects transcription of distal genes via its effect on long-range chromosomal interactions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the mechanistic findings.

claim: Chromatin accessibility affects transcription of distal genes via its effect on long-range chromosomal interactions.
source: Our results suggest that TF binding affects long-range chromosomal interactions via its effect on CA, and that CA affects transcription of distal genes via its effect on long-range chromosomal interactions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the mechanistic findings.

claim: Variants alter enhancer activities, which in turn alter the physical interactions of enhancers with distal genes, providing a molecular mechanism underlying distal eQTLs.
source: This latter inference is especially intriguing, since it suggests a molecular mechanism underlying distal eQTLs: variants alter enhancer activities, which in turn alter the physical interactions of enhancers with distal genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the mechanistic findings.

claim: This represents the first evidence that variation in the landscape of chromosomal interactions underlies long-range genetic effects on transcription.
source: To our knowledge, this represents the first evidence that variation in the landscape of chromosomal interactions underlies long-range genetic effects on transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The study has yet to map the majority of human caQTL variants, such as those specific to other cell types, those that affect chromatin accessibility of distal loci, or those involving rare variants or small effect sizes.
source: First, we have yet to map the majority of human caQTL variants—for example those specific to other cell types, those that affect CA of distal loci (in trans or long-range cis), or those involving rare variants or small effect sizes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the study.

claim: The shared caQTLs should be regarded only as candidate causal variants to guide future experiments.
source: Second, our shared caQTLs should be regarded only as candidate causal variants to guide future experiments, similar to other statistically fine-mapped associations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the study.

claim: The pooled approach can only map caQTLs that are covered by ATAC-seq reads.
source: Third, our fine-mapping approach is distinct from typical GWAS fine-mapping where many variants in a locus are genotyped in a large cohort; our pooled approach can only map caQTLs that are covered by ATAC-seq reads.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the study.

claim: Within regions of open chromatin, the pooled approach genotypes essentially all common variants.
source: Within these regions of open chromatin, our approach genotypes essentially all common variants, but variants outside these regions are not covered.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of the approach.

claim: The increased efficiency of the pooled approach resulted in over 10-fold more caQTLs than previous studies.
source: Despite this limitation, our increased efficiency resulted in over 10-fold more caQTLs than previous studies (Degner et al., 2012; Kumasaka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the comparison.

claim: Trans-ethnic fine-mapping will only work when a variant is present at an appreciable frequency and affects the same trait across multiple populations.
source: Fourth, like all forms of trans-ethnic fine-mapping, our method will only work when a variant is present at an appreciable frequency, and affects the same trait, across multiple populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the approach.

claim: Combining GWAS with pooled QTLs mapped in diverse populations and cell types will be an efficient and highly effective strategy for identifying causal variants and their molecular mechanisms of action.
source: Looking ahead, we expect that combining GWAS with pooled QTLs mapped in diverse populations and cell types will be an efficient and highly effective strategy for identifying causal variants and their molecular mechanisms of action, two major bottlenecks in bridging the gap between GWAS and disease etiologies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a forward-looking statement about the approach.
